source_user: A service receives a mix of short prompts and long generations. Design an evaluation plan that reports TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, and P99 latency. Scenario variant 294: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: separate prefill and decode behavior; fix workload distribution; report warmup; use repeated trials; capture GPU memory and request-level traces.
corrected_answer:
Scope: build a reproducible serving-evaluation harness for a mixed short-prompt / long-generation workload. Scenario variant 294. Emphasis: attribute each latency component to a mechanism (queue vs prefill vs decode vs interconnect) before proposing any tuning.

1) Assumptions (declare before any measurement)
- One model, one engine build (vLLM / SGLang / TensorRT-LLM, optionally fronted by NVIDIA Dynamo). Engine commit, CUDA, driver, NCCL and tokenizer versions pinned and recorded per arm.
- Fixed hardware topology: GPU count, TP/PP degree, NVLink vs PCIe intra-node, RoCE/IB inter-node if disaggregated. Topology is a factor, never an uncontrolled variable.
- Workload is a frozen, replayable trace: (input_len, output_len) pairs sampled once, hashed, and reused byte-identically across all arms. Never re-sample per arm.
- Metrics are client-observed unless explicitly labelled engine-internal.

2) Metric definitions (ambiguity here is the single largest source of bogus results)
- TTFT = client first-token-receive timestamp minus client request-send timestamp. Measuring from engine admission hides queueing and is the most common way TTFT is silently understated.
- TPOT = (last_token_ts - first_token_ts) / max(1, output_tokens - 1), reported per request, then aggregated.
- Queueing delay = admit_ts - arrival_ts, exported by the scheduler; must be reported separately, not folded into TTFT.
- Throughput reported as three distinct numbers: output tok/s, total (prefill+decode) tok/s, and completed req/s. A single "tok/s" figure is not comparable across arms with different length mixes.
- P99 computed over completed requests only, with the count of timed-out/rejected requests reported alongside; dropping failures inflates the tail percentile.

3) Load generation
- Open-loop, Poisson arrivals at a fixed target rate lambda. A closed-loop client with fixed concurrency suffers coordinated omission: when the server slows, the client stops offering load and P99 is structurally understated.
- Sweep lambda upward in steps until goodput saturates; report the full latency-vs-load curve, not one operating point. A single-point comparison is not falsifiable.
- Warmup: discard the first 60 s and the first 200 requests; CUDA graph capture, autotuning, allocator growth and prefix-cache fill all occur there.

4) Falsifiable hypothesis (variant 294)
H0: enabling chunked prefill with chunk size C at the fixed trace and lambda = 70% of measured saturation leaves P99 TTFT unchanged (difference within the bootstrap 95% CI) while degrading P99 TPOT by more than 15%.
H1: chunked prefill reduces P99 TTFT by >= 25% with P99 TPOT regression <= 10%.
Decision rule fixed in advance: reject H0 only if the P99 TTFT reduction's 95% bootstrap CI excludes 0 AND the TPOT regression CI upper bound stays under 10%. Pre-registering the rule prevents post-hoc metric shopping.

5) Controlled experiment
- Arms: A = baseline scheduler; B = chunked prefill (C swept over >= 3 values); optionally C = prefill/decode disaggregation. Exactly one factor changes per arm.
- >= 3 trials per cell, arms interleaved in time (A,B,A,B,...) so thermal drift and neighbour noise do not alias onto the arm variable.
- >= 2000 completed requests per cell; report bootstrap CIs on P50/P95/P99, not bare point estimates.
- Prefix caching: either disable it in all arms, or pin an identical cache-hit rate; an uncontrolled hit-rate delta can produce a fake 2x TTFT "win".

6) Expected confounders (each with a check)
- Coordinated omission -> verify open-loop arrival timestamps match the intended Poisson process (KS test).
- Client-side bottleneck -> client CPU < 70%, and client-observed send timestamps must not bunch.
- Thermal/power throttling -> DCGM clock-throttle reasons; discard cells with SW_POWER_CAP or HW_SLOWDOWN.
- Allocator fragmentation drift across long runs -> reset the process between cells.
- KV-cache pool sizing differing between arms -> assert identical gpu_memory_utilization / KV block count.
- Tokenizer mismatch changing effective token counts -> assert identical token counts for the frozen trace.
- Multi-node arms: NCCL algorithm/channel selection and RoCE PFC/ECN state must be captured; a paused link masquerades as a decode-speed regression.

7) Evidence to retain
Per-request trace (arrival, admit, first token, last token, in/out tokens, preemptions), scheduler queue-depth and preemption counters, prefix-cache hit rate, KV-pool occupancy, DCGM power/clock/throttle series, NVLink or RoCE counters, and the full config diff per arm. Trace file hash recorded in the report.

8) Rollback criteria (gate before any production change)
Canary at <= 5% traffic for >= 30 min. Auto-rollback if P99 TTFT worsens > 10%, P99 TPOT worsens > 10%, error/timeout rate > 0.1%, or preemption rate rises above baseline + 2x. Rollback is config-only (previous engine args + previous image tag) and must be exercised once in staging before the canary is trusted.

9) Limits
This plan yields a decision for this trace, this model, this topology. It does not generalise to a different length mix; re-run the harness when the workload distribution shifts materially (e.g. KS distance on output-length distribution > 0.1).

source_user: A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 1: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure per-request KV growth and allocator fragmentation; check max sequence and batch; inspect active sequences; test paged/prefix cache, admission control, quantization, and context limits.
corrected_answer:
Scope: intermittent OOM on a long-context workload appearing only after several concurrent requests. Scenario variant 1. Emphasis: the durable fix is admission control and an explicit memory budget, not one-off flag tuning.

0) Assumptions
- Single-node or TP-sharded deployment on a paged-attention engine (vLLM/SGLang class). Model dtype, TP degree, max_model_len, max_num_seqs and gpu_memory_utilization are known and recorded.
- "Intermittent, after several concurrent requests" is the key signal: it points at a demand-side term that scales with concurrency x sequence length (KV cache and activation peaks), not at a fixed weight-loading error. A deterministic OOM at startup would be a different failure class.

1) Mechanism: where the memory goes
Total = weights + KV cache pool + activation/workspace peak + fragmentation + non-torch allocations (NCCL buffers, CUDA graphs, cuBLAS workspace, comm buffers).
Per-token KV bytes = 2 (K and V) x num_layers x num_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element.
Per-request KV = per-token bytes x (prompt_len + generated_len). Under TP, KV heads are sharded, so per-GPU KV is divided by TP degree only when num_kv_heads is divisible by TP; GQA with few KV heads often replicates instead, which silently doubles or quadruples the expected per-GPU footprint. Compute this number explicitly for the deployed config — a large fraction of "mysterious" long-context OOM is arithmetic that was never done.
Note the concurrency coupling: the pool is sized once at startup, so OOM appearing only under concurrency usually means either (a) the paged pool is exhausted and the engine should preempt but a non-paged allocation is racing it, or (b) the true OOM is in the activation/workspace peak during a large prefill batch, not in the KV pool at all.

2) Falsifiable hypothesis (variant 1)
H0: the OOM is driven by the transient prefill activation peak, not by KV-pool exhaustion. Prediction: capping the per-step batched prefill token budget (chunked prefill / max_num_batched_tokens) to <= 4096 eliminates OOM at unchanged max_num_seqs and unchanged KV-pool size, and torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated peak drops by >= 20%.
H1 (alternative): the OOM is KV-pool exhaustion or fragmentation. Prediction: capping prefill tokens does NOT help, while lowering max_num_seqs or raising the pool does.
These make opposite predictions under the same intervention, so one experiment discriminates them.

3) Controlled experiment
- Replay a fixed trace that reproduces the OOM within a bounded time (record trace hash and reproduction rate over >= 5 runs; if reproduction is < 100%, all conclusions need the same repetition count).
- Arm A: baseline. Arm B: max_num_batched_tokens = 4096, everything else identical. Arm C: max_num_seqs halved, everything else identical.
- One factor per arm; >= 5 replays per arm; report OOM occurrence rate with a binomial CI, not a single pass/fail.
- Instrument torch.cuda.memory_stats() (allocated, reserved, active, inactive_split) and dump a memory snapshot at the failing step.

4) Prioritised diagnosis and mitigations (cheapest/most reversible first)
1. Compute the KV budget arithmetically and compare with the pool actually allocated. Fix a wrong max_model_len or a GQA/TP sharding assumption. Zero risk, config-only.
2. Bound the prefill token budget (chunked prefill). Trades a small TTFT increase for a bounded activation peak. Reversible.
3. Enable/verify admission control: reject or queue when projected KV demand exceeds free blocks, rather than admitting and OOM-ing. This converts a crash into backpressure — the correct operational behaviour.
4. Address fragmentation: set PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True and confirm reserved-minus-allocated shrinks. Only meaningful if the snapshot shows large inactive_split blocks; otherwise it is cargo cult.
5. Verify prefix/paged cache is actually on and that block size and eviction are sane; a disabled paged cache reintroduces contiguous per-request allocation.
6. Lower max_model_len or max_num_seqs to a value the budget arithmetic supports. This is a capability reduction and needs product sign-off.
7. KV quantization (fp8) or a smaller-KV model variant. Last resort: it changes output quality and requires a separate accuracy gate before rollout.

5) Confounders
- Other processes on the same GPU (MPS, monitoring, a stale worker) consuming memory -> check nvidia-smi per-process usage.
- CUDA graph capture reserving memory after warmup, so the first OOM appears minutes in.
- NCCL/comm buffers growing with TP degree and message size (multi-node).
- Memory growth from a leak in the request path, distinguishable because it rises monotonically across runs rather than tracking concurrency.
- Preemption/recompute masking the problem as a latency spike in some runs and an OOM in others.

6) Evidence required
Per-request prompt/generation lengths at failure, KV blocks free/used over time, torch memory snapshot at the failing step, engine preemption counters, nvidia-smi per-process memory, engine config dump, and the reproduction rate over >= 5 replays.

7) Rollback criteria
Any mitigation ships behind a canary at <= 5% traffic. Auto-rollback if OOM recurs at all, if P99 TTFT worsens > 15%, or if rejection rate exceeds 0.5%. Steps 6 and 7 additionally require an accuracy/functional gate because they change model behaviour, not just resource limits.

corrected_answer:
Scope: intermittent OOM on a long-context workload appearing only after several concurrent requests. Scenario variant 4. Emphasis: the durable fix is admission control and an explicit memory budget, not one-off flag tuning.

0) Assumptions
- Single-node or TP-sharded deployment on a paged-attention engine (vLLM/SGLang class). Model dtype, TP degree, max_model_len, max_num_seqs and gpu_memory_utilization are known and recorded.
- "Intermittent, after several concurrent requests" is the key signal: it points at a demand-side term that scales with concurrency x sequence length (KV cache and activation peaks), not at a fixed weight-loading error. A deterministic OOM at startup would be a different failure class.

1) Mechanism: where the memory goes
Total = weights + KV cache pool + activation/workspace peak + fragmentation + non-torch allocations (NCCL buffers, CUDA graphs, cuBLAS workspace, comm buffers).
Per-token KV bytes = 2 (K and V) x num_layers x num_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element.
Per-request KV = per-token bytes x (prompt_len + generated_len). Under TP, KV heads are sharded, so per-GPU KV is divided by TP degree only when num_kv_heads is divisible by TP; GQA with few KV heads often replicates instead, which silently doubles or quadruples the expected per-GPU footprint. Compute this number explicitly for the deployed config — a large fraction of "mysterious" long-context OOM is arithmetic that was never done.
Note the concurrency coupling: the pool is sized once at startup, so OOM appearing only under concurrency usually means either (a) the paged pool is exhausted and the engine should preempt but a non-paged allocation is racing it, or (b) the true OOM is in the activation/workspace peak during a large prefill batch, not in the KV pool at all.

2) Falsifiable hypothesis (variant 4)
H0: the OOM is driven by the transient prefill activation peak, not by KV-pool exhaustion. Prediction: capping the per-step batched prefill token budget (chunked prefill / max_num_batched_tokens) to <= 4096 eliminates OOM at unchanged max_num_seqs and unchanged KV-pool size, and torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated peak drops by >= 20%.
H1 (alternative): the OOM is KV-pool exhaustion or fragmentation. Prediction: capping prefill tokens does NOT help, while lowering max_num_seqs or raising the pool does.
These make opposite predictions under the same intervention, so one experiment discriminates them.

3) Controlled experiment
- Replay a fixed trace that reproduces the OOM within a bounded time (record trace hash and reproduction rate over >= 5 runs; if reproduction is < 100%, all conclusions need the same repetition count).
- Arm A: baseline. Arm B: max_num_batched_tokens = 4096, everything else identical. Arm C: max_num_seqs halved, everything else identical.
- One factor per arm; >= 5 replays per arm; report OOM occurrence rate with a binomial CI, not a single pass/fail.
- Instrument torch.cuda.memory_stats() (allocated, reserved, active, inactive_split) and dump a memory snapshot at the failing step.

4) Prioritised diagnosis and mitigations (cheapest/most reversible first)
1. Compute the KV budget arithmetically and compare with the pool actually allocated. Fix a wrong max_model_len or a GQA/TP sharding assumption. Zero risk, config-only.
2. Bound the prefill token budget (chunked prefill). Trades a small TTFT increase for a bounded activation peak. Reversible.
3. Enable/verify admission control: reject or queue when projected KV demand exceeds free blocks, rather than admitting and OOM-ing. This converts a crash into backpressure — the correct operational behaviour.
4. Address fragmentation: set PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True and confirm reserved-minus-allocated shrinks. Only meaningful if the snapshot shows large inactive_split blocks; otherwise it is cargo cult.
5. Verify prefix/paged cache is actually on and that block size and eviction are sane; a disabled paged cache reintroduces contiguous per-request allocation.
6. Lower max_model_len or max_num_seqs to a value the budget arithmetic supports. This is a capability reduction and needs product sign-off.
7. KV quantization (fp8) or a smaller-KV model variant. Last resort: it changes output quality and requires a separate accuracy gate before rollout.

5) Confounders
- Other processes on the same GPU (MPS, monitoring, a stale worker) consuming memory -> check nvidia-smi per-process usage.
- CUDA graph capture reserving memory after warmup, so the first OOM appears minutes in.
- NCCL/comm buffers growing with TP degree and message size (multi-node).
- Memory growth from a leak in the request path, distinguishable because it rises monotonically across runs rather than tracking concurrency.
- Preemption/recompute masking the problem as a latency spike in some runs and an OOM in others.

6) Evidence required
Per-request prompt/generation lengths at failure, KV blocks free/used over time, torch memory snapshot at the failing step, engine preemption counters, nvidia-smi per-process memory, engine config dump, and the reproduction rate over >= 5 replays.

7) Rollback criteria
Any mitigation ships behind a canary at <= 5% traffic. Auto-rollback if OOM recurs at all, if P99 TTFT worsens > 15%, or if rejection rate exceeds 0.5%. Steps 6 and 7 additionally require an accuracy/functional gate because they change model behaviour, not just resource limits.
risks: Source answer is a rubric listing checkpoints; it gives no KV-memory arithmetic and no way to decide between competing causes.
No falsifiable hypothesis distinguishing prefill activation peak from KV-pool exhaustion, so the listed mitigations would be applied blindly and simultaneously.
Mitigations are listed without risk ordering: lowering max_model_len and KV quantization change user-visible capability/quality and are not config-only rollbacks.
GQA/TP KV-head sharding subtlety omitted; assuming KV always divides by TP degree understates per-GPU footprint.
No admission-control recommendation, so the failure mode stays a crash instead of backpressure.
No reproduction-rate requirement, so an intermittent fault can appear 'fixed' by chance.
evidence_required: Explicit KV-byte arithmetic for the deployed config (layers, num_kv_heads, head_dim, dtype, TP degree) vs the pool actually allocated
Fixed replay trace that reproduces OOM, with hash and reproduction rate over >=5 runs
torch.cuda.memory_stats() and a memory snapshot captured at the failing step
KV blocks free/used time series and engine preemption counters
nvidia-smi per-process memory to rule out co-tenant consumption
Engine config dump (max_model_len, max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens, gpu_memory_utilization) per arm
Accuracy/functional gate results if KV quantization or context truncation is adopted
